metadata.title: Product Streams
metadata.description: Outcome-based product streams for the BI Dashboard Extensions Platform domain: the lifecycle Discover -> Trial -> Build -> Use -> Distribute -> Deploy -> Govern -> Renew as run by dashboard creators, BI platform leads, business users, planners, executives, IT administrators, security reviewers and partners on the Infotopics | Apps for Tableau extension portfolio across Tableau, Power BI and Looker Studio.
metadata.flowModelNote: Each stream carries only stream-specific flows, names the supporting bricks used in each step and the persona acting in it, and lists the external systems (Tableau Cloud/Server and Desktop, Tableau Exchange and Microsoft AppSource, the customer's databases and identity provider, Teams/Slack and email, vendor-risk and certification parties, payment and CRM) the flow depends on.

rootGroups.name: Acquisition and Building Journeys
rootGroups.description: From discovery and trial to published, extension-powered dashboards: the journeys that bring an organisation onto the extensions and put them into creators' hands.

streams.name: Discover, Trial and Subscribe to Extensions
streams.description: Take a dashboard creator or BI platform lead from first contact — the website, the Tableau Exchange, Microsoft AppSource, a partner or a conference demo — to a working Free plan, a WriteBackExtreme trial and a paid Professional or Enterprise subscription, and keep that subscription renewing year after year without a sales-heavy motion the 30-person company cannot afford.
outcomes: Creators reach a working extension in their own dashboard within minutes of signup, without a credit card or a sales call
Free-plan organisations convert to Professional and Enterprise when they cross five active users, because the plan ladder is visible in the product and the portal
Every subscription carries the right plan, user count, deployment model and support level, so renewals are a confirmation instead of a negotiation
Partner-sourced and marketplace-sourced signups are attributed correctly, so deal registration and margin are honoured

flows.title: From Website Signup to an Enterprise Subscription
flows.description: A creator finds SuperTables, signs up for the Free plan, rolls it out to colleagues, trials WriteBackExtreme and finally moves the organisation to an Enterprise subscription with an on-premises option.
flows.trigger: A creator searches for an Excel-like table for Tableau, lands on appsfortableau.infotopics.com or the Tableau Exchange listing and opens the SuperTables product page.
flows.successSignal: The organisation holds an Enterprise subscription with license keys in the Enterprise Customer Portal and a dedicated customer success manager assigned.

steps.title: Discover the extension on the website, Exchange or via a partner
keyFacts: The website, the Tableau Exchange listing, Microsoft AppSource and 32 partners are the four discovery routes; the gallery shows each of the 30+ extensions in a live demo workbook.
Named customers such as Bank of America, Pfizer, Siemens and Johnson & Johnson and the Post Holdings quote about Excel-minded users are the social proof a creator forwards to a sceptical lead.
painPoints: Creators cannot tell which extensions are SaaS-only, Enterprise-only (WriteBackExtreme, MailScheduler) or available for Power BI without reading several pages.
A creator who finds the extension in the Exchange may never see the pricing page and assumes it is free forever.

steps.title: Sign up for the Free plan without a credit card

Users are counted as anyone interacting with a published dashboard — creators, explorers and viewers — via anonymous unique tokens over a rolling 12 months.
painPoints: Corporate email domains are sometimes already registered by a colleague, creating duplicate organisation accounts that later complicate licensing.
Creators expect an install step and do not realise the SaaS-hosted extension only needs safelisting on their Tableau site.

streams.name: Build Interactive Dashboards With Extensions
streams.description: Take a dashboard creator from a business requirement — an Excel-minded team asking for one more variant of the same dashboard — to a published, governed dashboard in Tableau Cloud, Tableau Server, Power BI or Looker Studio with configured SuperTables, ShowMeMore charts, PowerKPIs, PictureThis, HierarchyFilter and design helpers, so that one dashboard satisfies many audiences.
outcomes: One interactive dashboard replaces the five to ten static variants a creator used to maintain for different audiences
Extension configuration is done in the dashboard and persisted in the workbook, so no separate admin tool or code is needed
Dashboards survive publishing: the same extension works in Desktop, on Tableau Cloud and on a safelisted Tableau Server
The same configuration model carries to Power BI and Looker Studio, so multi-platform organisations do not rebuild

flows.title: Configure SuperTables in Desktop and Publish to Tableau Cloud
flows.description: A creator turns a request for 'the dashboard but in Excel' into a SuperTables-based dashboard, configures it in Tableau Desktop and publishes it to a Tableau Cloud site where the extension is safelisted.
flows.trigger: A finance team asks for the fourth variant of a sales dashboard with different columns, subtotals and an export button.
flows.successSignal: The published dashboard is opened by the requesting team on Tableau Cloud and they pivot, group and export without a new request.

steps.title: Capture the requirement as one interactive table instead of variants
keyFacts: Typical asks are column choice, subtotals, conditional formatting, formulas and Excel export — all things a SuperTable exposes to the viewer at runtime.
A Post Holdings senior director with 1,000+ Tableau users described SuperTables as making Tableau accessible to people used to Excel.
painPoints: Creators default to building another worksheet per request because that is what Tableau natively supports.
Business users describe the need as 'just export to Excel', hiding the real need to explore.

steps.title: Add the extension object and connect it to a worksheet
keyFacts: The extension is added as a dashboard object from the .trex manifest or the Exchange; the data connector reads a hidden or visible worksheet and syncs its filters and parameters.
The server-side row model handles millions of rows by paging and aggregating on the server instead of the browser.
painPoints: Worksheet field naming and hidden-sheet conventions differ per creator, making configurations hard to hand over.
Large worksheets time out in the browser when the creator forgets to enable the server-side row model.

rootGroups.name: Dashboard Use and Decision Journeys
rootGroups.description: The journeys business users, planners and executives run inside and around the dashboard: self-service exploration, governed write-back and planning, financial reporting, scheduled distribution, and guided adoption.

streams.name: Explore and Self-Serve Data in Dashboards
streams.description: Take a business dashboard viewer from a question — why is this region below budget, which products drive the variance, what happened in this process — to an answer inside the published dashboard: pivot, group, filter, drill down, follow a process view, save a personal view and export to Excel, without raising a new dashboard request.
outcomes: Viewers answer their own follow-up questions inside the dashboard, so new dashboard requests per user fall
Excel-minded users adopt the governed dashboard instead of exporting raw data and rebuilding it in spreadsheets
Personal saved views let each viewer keep their own layout while the data and security stay governed
Exports carry the current filters, groupings and formatting, so the numbers in a meeting match the dashboard

flows.title: Answer a Variance Question Inside the Dashboard
flows.description: A viewer opens a published sales dashboard, narrows to their region, pivots by product and customer, drills into a hierarchy, saves the view and exports to Excel for a meeting.
flows.trigger: The monthly sales dashboard shows a region below target and the regional manager wants to know why before the Monday meeting.
flows.successSignal: The manager arrives at the meeting with a saved view and an Excel export that reconcile to the dashboard, and has not asked the BI team for anything.

steps.title: Open the dashboard and narrow to the relevant hierarchy
keyFacts: The extension loads within the published dashboard on Tableau Cloud or Server; a HierarchyFilter narrows region, country and sales office in one control.
Filter and parameter changes are synchronised both ways between the extension and the native worksheets.
painPoints: Viewers do not realise the table is interactive and treat it as a static crosstab.
Slow initial loads on large worksheets discourage exploration.

Conditional formatting configured by the creator highlights variances against target.
painPoints: Users pivot into combinations the creator never anticipated and find data-quality issues.
Aggregations of already aggregated worksheet measures can mislead if the creator did not set the aggregation type.

keyFacts: DrillDownTree expands category, subcategory and SKU level by level; the selection acts on the rest of the dashboard.
Drill paths follow the hierarchy defined in the data source, so governance is preserved.
painPoints: Deep hierarchies with thousands of leaves need lazy loading or the tree becomes unusable.
Viewers lose track of where they are after several drills.

Generative fill can propose values for a column from the pattern in other rows, subject to the creator's settings.
painPoints: Business users need to know which numbers are computed and which are generated text before they quote them.
Security reviewers want assurance that dashboard data sent for AI processing stays within agreed boundaries.

Views persist across sessions and are tied to the viewer's Tableau identity.
painPoints: Viewers assume saved views are shared and are surprised when a colleague cannot see them.
Workbook republishes with renamed fields break saved views silently.

painPoints: Exports of millions of rows are blocked or slow, and viewers do not understand why.
Once exported, numbers get edited in Excel and re-circulated as if they were the dashboard.
